title: extract does not re-verify blob digests: a tampered store blob extracts cleanly (invariant gap, not a threat-model bypass)
body:
### What you did, what happened, what you expected

What I did: pulled `alpine:latest` with the shipped beta (`podbox-v0.1.0-beta.1-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, sha256 `42e34c3a...51cf2`), then flipped one byte inside the stored layer blob's file-content region in the store, then ran `podbox extract alpine:latest` after removing the existing rootfs. Also drove the same scenario in-process against podbox-extract's own public API (uncompressed tar layer, one-byte content flip).

What happened: extraction succeeded and the payload-visible file carried the tampered bytes. The manifest still named the original digest.

What I expected: per SECURITY.md "Invariants", "A blob is accepted only when its computed digest matches the manifest". That invariant does not hold on the extract path.

Scope statement up front: this is not a threat-model bypass. SECURITY.md explicitly makes the store the operator's authority and puts post-compromise protection out of scope. The finding is that a stated invariant is not enforced on one path, and the read-side re-verification that store.rs already has (`read_blob`) is not used by extract.

### How to reproduce it

Binary repro (beta asset, any Linux host):

```sh
podbox pull alpine:latest
podbox extract alpine:latest          # first extract is fine
# remove the extracted rootfs but keep the store
rm -rf "$HOME/.local/share/podbox/rootfs/sha256_d56c381f961d307a21b3ca004cf1e3910f106644aefb1f43e654c8a56c4fd395"
# tamper: flip one byte inside the layer blob's content
LAYER="$HOME/.local/share/podbox/blobs/sha256/e2de96513ba9eb53b431787ec8a65cdde380ac4772a3e4c4b714dcfde2a102b5"
printf 'X' | dd of="$LAYER" bs=1 seek=514 conv=notrunc   # offset inside a file's data block
podbox extract alpine:latest && echo "EXTRACTED TAMPERED BYTES"
```

In-process repro (deterministic, uses the crate's own store scaffolding, uncompressed tar so gzip CRC cannot be the thing that catches it): I built a one-entry tar, committed it through `Store::put_bytes` (verified on the way in), flipped the byte at offset 514 in the stored blob, and called `podbox_extract::extract` with a manifest naming the ORIGINAL digest.

Result: `EXTRACTED OK: entries=1 good.txt="heLlo"` where the honest content was `"hello"`.

### Code path

- `crates/podbox-extract/src/lib.rs`, `extract_layers()`: opens each layer with `layer::open(blob, c)`.
- `crates/podbox-extract/src/layer.rs`, `open()`: plain `File::open` + decompressor. No digest recomputation.
- `crates/podbox-image/src/store.rs`, `read_blob()` DOES re-verify on the way out, but extract never calls it; it goes through `store.blob_path()` and reads the file directly.
- Net effect: gzip layers are protected only by gzip's own CRC (my corrupted-blob test was caught as "corrupt deflate stream" because the flip landed mid-stream), zstd by ruzstd's frame checks, and uncompressed tar layers by nothing at all.

### Suggested fixes (pick one, or scope it explicitly)

1. Hash each blob while streaming it into the decompressor in `extract_layers` and compare against the manifest digest before applying entries. One pass, no extra I/O.
2. Or call `Store::read_blob` on the extract path and accept the double read.
3. Or amend SECURITY.md's invariant to say digest parity is enforced at pull time only, so the document stops claiming more than the code does.

Measured 2026-09-22 on the v0.1.0-beta.1 asset and on a rebuild of commit 1430040. Environment: Linux 6.18.39 x86_64, uid 0 with empty capability bounding set (podbox's own target class of host), rustc 1.98.1.

title: committed Cargo.lock is stale vs the manifests: every fresh build dirties the tree, so the binary self-reports -dirty (explains the beta asset)
body:
### What you did, what happened, what you expected

What I did: cloned the repo at the release commit `8d9dbd70`, ran `scripts/build-interpose.sh`, then `cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, then `podbox version --verbose`.

What happened: the binary reports `commit: 8d9dbd70...-dirty`, and `git status` shows `M Cargo.lock`, on a tree that was pristine (`git status --porcelain` printed nothing) before the build.

What I expected: a build of a clean checkout should leave the tree clean and the recorded commit should be `8d9dbd70...` without `-dirty`.

This is the explanation for why the released beta asset announces `-dirty`: the release notes say the binary "reports that commit with `-dirty` for the lane copy, and the crate sources are identical to it", but no lane copy is needed to produce the suffix. Any fresh build produces it.

### How to reproduce it

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Azathothas/podbox && cd podbox
git checkout 8d9dbd70b94b4fd703dea051f0c686eb21f9a0b4
git status --porcelain | wc -l        # 0
./scripts/build-interpose.sh          # optional; the lock rewrite is the point
cargo build --release                 # or --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
git status --porcelain                #  M Cargo.lock
./target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/podbox version --verbose | head -2
# commit: 8d9dbd70...-dirty
```

### Mechanism

The committed `Cargo.lock` is stale against the committed manifests:

- `crates/podbox-cli/Cargo.toml` declares `sha2.workspace = true`, but the committed lock's `podbox-cli` dependency list has no `sha2`.
- `crates/podbox-image/Cargo.toml` declares `base64.workspace = true`, but the committed lock's `podbox-image` list has no `base64`.

Cargo resolves the graph on the first build and rewrites the lock, which modifies a tracked file, which `build.rs`'s `git status --porcelain` sees, so the binary records `-dirty`. Verified end to end on a pristine clone.

Side effect worth caring about: `experiments/120-reproducible-build.sh` compares two builds' hashes in the lane, where the second build starts from an already-rewritten lock; on a fresh clone the lock rewrite is exactly the kind of input drift that measurement exists to catch. T-1004's own text says "where they do not, name what differed rather than dropping the claim".

### Fix

`cargo update -p podbox-cli -p podbox-image --workspace` (or just `cargo check` then commit) the lock so it matches the manifests, in its own change. Also worth deciding whether `build.rs` should record dirtiness from tracked-file changes that cargo itself caused; today the field cannot distinguish "hand-edited source" from "cargo rewrote the lock".

title: no entry path exists when chroot(2) itself is denied: probe says interpose is permitted but every rung, including forced memfd, dies at chroot EPERM
body:
### What you did, what happened, what you expected

What I did: ran the shipped beta on a host where `chroot(2)` itself is denied (uid 0 but empty capability bounding set, seccomp-filtered). Ran `podbox probe`, then `podbox run alpine:latest /bin/echo hi`, then `PODBOX_MODE=memfd podbox run` with a static payload placed in the rootfs.

What happened: probe selects `interpose` ("this machine would permit `interpose`"), but every entry path dies at `chroot(".")` with EPERM, exit 125, including the forced memfd rung, which never uses a path but still chroots first. `podbox start` on a created container fails the same way. Net: on exactly the class of host the README names first ("restricted environments where uid 0 is present but namespaces, mounts, device creation, and ownership changes may be denied"), a host that additionally denies chroot cannot launch any payload at all.

What I expected: either the ladder to have a rung that reaches the payload without `chroot(2)` (the interposer's own mechanism makes one possible), or the parity/probe layer to refuse `run` up front naming "chroot denied" instead of a launch failure after fixups have already run, or a documented statement that chroot-denied hosts are out of scope. Today the README's promise ("probes the host before choosing an execution rung") stops one rung short of where this class of host actually is.

### How to reproduce it

On any host with chroot denied (no CAP_SYS_CHROOT and seccomp filtering it, or a user namespace without it mapped):

```sh
podbox probe
#   ... chroot=EPERM
#   "this machine would permit `interpose`"
podbox pull alpine:latest
podbox run alpine:latest /bin/echo hi
#   podbox run: the payload could not be started: chroot(".") failed with EPERM (1)
#   exit 125, after fixups, interpose placement, and the banner have all run
PODBOX_MODE=memfd podbox run alpine:latest /hello    # static binary copied into the rootfs
#   "entering on the memfd rung at PODBOX_MODE's request"
#   podbox run: the payload could not be started: chroot(".") failed with EPERM (1)
```

The entry sequence in `crates/podbox-enter/src/lib.rs` is fchdir/chroot/chdir by design (T-0502), and the ladder rungs (memfd, fuse, tmpfs, rundir, cache) change WHERE the payload bytes come from, not whether a chroot happens. The interposer is already placed into the rootfs and the identity memo machinery exists, but nothing can execute the payload because the runtime refuses to change root.

### What I am actually asking for

One of:

1. A no-chroot rung (probe-driven like the others): without CAP_SYS_CHROOT, skip the chroot and run the payload against the rootfs with the interposer providing path/ownership virtualization. It is strictly weaker than today's chroot rung and the existing honesty machinery (banner, `--strict`, parity table) is exactly the right place to say so. The refused-rung table in `podbox probe` already has all the legs needed to gate it.
2. Or an explicit refusal for `run`/`start`/`create` when the entered rung's syscall is denied, naming it up front (before completion fixups mutate the rootfs), instead of a 125 after the work.
3. Or a line in README/SECURITY.md: hosts that deny chroot(2) are unsupported. That is a defensible scoping decision, but it should be written down, because the probe result on such a host currently reads as if interpose tier will carry it.

Environment: Linux 6.18.39 x86_64, uid 0, CapEff 0000000000000000, NoNewPrivs 1, seccomp 2, openat2 present, rustc 1.98.1 (the project's own pinned toolchain). Full `podbox probe` output available on request.

title: release integrity: beta.1's build commit failed the repo's own gate, and the released bytes do not reproduce outside the lane while the notes read as if they do
body:
### The problem

Two release-integrity gaps on `v0.1.0-beta.1`, both about the release not carrying the evidence the project elsewhere insists on.

**1. The tagged commit failed the repo's own gate.** The tag points at `53b082b`, and the parent `8d9dbd7` is the commit the binary was built from. CI on `8d9dbd7` (run 35755156697, push to main) failed the "TODO index and citations" check:

```
check-todo: 1 problem(s)
  TODO/packaging.md:113: (T-1003) closes without a recorded run: the first
  unindented line after Prove does not open with `**Done`. TODO/gate.md T-1208.
```

`main` and the tag's own check runs show green because the fix landed in `53b082b`/`1b8946f` minutes later, but the release's build commit shipped with the repo's own consistency gate red. Given this project's discipline ("a count that disagrees with the rows cannot reach a commit"), the beta's binary should have been rebuilt from a commit the gate passed, or the release notes should say the gate state of the commit they name.

**2. Non-reproducing build, stated as reproducible.** The release says the crate sources are identical to the build commit, and T-1004 is closed as "two builds of one commit match byte for byte". Both are true in the lane. But:

- Building `8d9dbd7` on a different host (same rustc 1.98.1, same zig 0.16.0 with matching sha256) gives `3df62208d2991f0154c93f69739dcfc821bdaeac4cb886f03f74924b89533cf0`, not the released `42e34c3ae634f2c3e8ea083152aa6350f6be734b03e5ea04362cecc775a51cf2`.
- Two of my builds on one host are byte-identical to each other, so the tree is deterministic; the cross-host difference is the embedded glibc interposer object: my rebuild reports `interpose-gnu: 7751e26e...`, the released asset reports `96f50922...`, while `interpose-musl` matches exactly (`895b3b07...`). The gnu object embeds the build host's glibc version symbols (`objdump`-derived version gates in `interpose.map`), so it is host-sensitive by construction.
- The released binary also self-reports `-dirty` (see issue #11: the committed lock is stale, so any fresh build dirties the tree), which the release notes paper over as "the lane copy".

None of this is dishonest in intent; T-1004's wording ("verify that two builds of the same commit on the same toolchain produce the same bytes") is technically met. But a reader who downloads the beta and wants to verify the supply chain has no path that ends in the released bytes, and the project's own standard is that claims carry their conditions.

### What you have in mind

- Release notes (or `version --verbose`) should state the gate state of the build commit.
- State the reproducibility boundary in one line: "byte-identical within one host/toolchain; cross-host builds differ in the embedded glibc interposer object (digest reported in `version --verbose`)". The `interpose-musl` object being stable cross-host while glibc is not is itself worth one sentence in T-1004.
- Consider building the interposer objects against pinned/floating upstream glibc headers rather than the build host's, if cross-host reproducibility is ever wanted for real.

### What you tried instead

Checked whether the difference was my tree (it was not: pristine clone, same commit, `git status` clean before build), toolchain (matched the pinned zig sha256 and rustc), and the lock-rewrite issue (#11), which explains only the `-dirty` suffix, not the byte difference.

title: podbox cp cannot touch an image's extracted rootfs, so restricted hosts (and any pre-start workflow) have no checked way to stage or retrieve files
body:
### The problem

`podbox cp` only works against container records, and `podbox run` leaves no record, so on a host where the payload cannot launch (see issue #12) there is no way to move files in or out of an extracted rootfs except by hand-editing the store directory. That is the workflow gap, but the sharper finding is the reverse: the only interface that reaches the rootfs with containment checks is gated on a successfully started container, which is the one thing restricted hosts cannot always provide.

The README names CI executors and HPC nodes as target users. Both routinely need to stage files into an image and pull results out, before or without any long-running container.

### What you have in mind

Three options, in increasing scope:

1. Let `podbox cp` accept `image:path` (the extracted rootfs in the store) as well as `container:path`, reusing the existing containment-checked path unchanged.
2. A `podbox stage <image> <src...>` / `podbox unstage` pair (no docker parity debt; it is podbox's own verb like `probe` and `extract`).
3. Document the store-layout workaround in docs/ so nobody reads `podbox cp`'s refusal as "no files in or out, ever".

The containment machinery (`podbox-extract`'s `safety` module) is already there to make option 1 safe; nothing new has to be trusted.

### What you tried instead

`podbox cp alpine:latest:/etc/os-release /tmp/x` (refused: "no such container: alpine"), `create` + `cp` (works but only where `start` works, which it does not on chroot-denied hosts), and raw writes into `$store/rootfs/<digest>/rootfs` (works, but bypasses every check the project built and requires knowing the digest).

title: no store-health verb (verify) and no pull provenance: digests are enforced per-read but nothing sweeps the store or records where bytes came from
body:
### The problem

`podbox images`/`pull`/`extract` verify digests, but nothing today helps an operator answer "is the store healthy, and how did the digests get there?" Two concrete gaps seen while reviewing and testing:

1. **No `podbox verify`.** `Store::read_blob` re-verifies on read, but a sweep command that hashes every blob in the store and diffs against the index would catch store corruption, partial writes, or bit-rot in one command. `experiments/210-store-concurrency.sh` has exactly this loop in its `verify()` shell function, so the logic is already written; it is just not a product verb. `podbox system info` reports store location; there is no store-health surface at all.
2. **No provenance record for pulled blobs.** Pull writes blobs and an index entry, but no record of which registry, tag, manifest digest, and time a blob came from beyond what the index implies. The corpus standard this repo holds itself to (pinned inputs, recorded provenance, `docs/methodology/experiments.md`) argues for the same on the store: one JSON line per manifest pulled (`registry, repository, tag, manifest digest, pulled-at, podbox version`).

### What you have in mind

- `podbox verify [image|all]`: hash every blob (or one image's blobs), compare against index digests, print one line per mismatch and a summary, exit non-zero on any mismatch. The `verify()` function in experiments/210 is the starting shape.
- Store provenance as sidecar JSON next to the index (not inside image metadata), so scripts can answer "where did this rootfs come from and when" without parsing registry URLs out of nothing.

### What you tried instead

`podbox images`, `podbox inspect`, and `podbox system info`: none report store health or pull provenance. Shell `sha256sum` over `blobs/sha256/*` works for a manual audit (filenames are the digests, which is a nice property worth keeping) but nothing consumes the result.

title: four parity-table gaps have no TODO entries: save/load/import, logs -f, cp directories, launcher signal forwarding
body:
### The problem

Four workflow features are named as unimplemented in the parity table but have no TODO entry tracking them, so they can silently stay missing across milestones. Checked against `TODO/INDEX.md` on 2026-09-22 (commit 1430040), each has no entry anywhere in TODO/:

1. **`docker save` / `load` / `import`**. The parity rows say it plainly: `save`: "the store holds OCI blobs and nothing exports them yet"; `load`: "`pull` is the only way into the store"; `import`: nothing builds a record from a rootfs tar. For the named audience (CI executors, HPC nodes, air-gapped hosts) registry-only image ingress is a real limit: a host with no registry reachability cannot receive an image at all, and there is no way to hand a podbox-built store to another host. Even one direction (an `OCI-layout` directory or tarball in/out) would close most of it, and the store is already content-addressed, so `save` is close to a tar of `blobs/` + index + manifest.

2. **`logs -f`**. The `logs` row says "`-f` is not implemented (T-0605)". T-0605 covers capture-at-spawn; following (a tail loop or inotify on the container's log file, bounded like the rest of the lifecycle verbs) has no entry. Automated callers polling `logs` in a loop is the current workaround.

3. **`cp` of directories**. "one file at a time, either way". A recursive option with the same containment checks (the extract safety module already has the walker) has no entry.

4. **Signal forwarding to the payload on launcher shutdown**. `stop`/`kill` reach the payload by pidfd, and the `stop` row honestly says reparented grandchildren are out of reach. But the inverse case, the launcher itself receiving SIGINT/SIGTERM (Ctrl-C on a foreground `podbox run`) and forwarding to the payload before exiting, has no entry either way. If the design is "the payload dies with the launcher via PR_SET_PDEATHSIG" (T-0603 exists), then one parity-table sentence naming that mechanism would close the question; if not, it needs an entry.

None of these four is a complaint about honesty; the parity table is admirably exact about each one. The gap is bookkeeping: RULES.md says nothing closes as "out of scope", but these are not recorded as open either, so no future session will find them in the work order.

### What you have in mind

Four entries (or one entry with four halves) in TODO/cli.md / TODO/image.md, P2-P3, each naming the parity row it would upgrade and the acceptance command shape. The point is that the TODO index is the only work order, and these four are only visible in code comments today.

title: experiments/210 misclassifies registry HTTP 429 as a store-contract failure, and its prune check cannot distinguish a chroot-denied host from a deleted rootfs
body:
### What you did, what happened, what you expected

What I did: ran `experiments/210-store-concurrency.sh` twice on a restricted host (uid 0, chroot denied, kernel 6.18.39), then re-ran a modified copy that preserved its work directory so the failing worker's output could be read.

What happened: exit 1 with `FAIL: a worker exited non-zero for a reason that is not the network`. The failing worker's actual output was `HTTP 429: TOOMANYREQUESTS: Rate exceeded` from `public.ecr.aws`. The harness's network-failure grep covers `connect|resolve|timed out|tls|certificate`, so a rate-limit (an HTTP-level refusal, not a connection failure) reads as a contract failure.

What I expected: a 429 from the registry to read as SKIP (quota), same as a connect failure. The script's own comment says "A network failure is not a contract failure, and the two must not be collapsed"; a rate limit is on the network side of that line.

Second, same family: check 2's FAIL lines (`the payload died while a prune ran`, `prune did not name what it skipped`) are also environmental on a chroot-denied host: the holder payload exits 125 because `chroot(".")` is denied, which looks identical to prune having deleted its rootfs. The script cannot currently distinguish "holder died because prune removed its rootfs" from "holder died because it could not start at all on this host".

Reproducibility: 125 appeared once in check 1's eight workers on each of three runs (position varied: w4, w3, w2), consistent with one worker hitting the rate limit each time, not with a store race (which would not show an HTTP 429 in the failing worker's transcript).

### How to reproduce it

```sh
./experiments/210-store-concurrency.sh      # on a host behind an ECR rate limit
# exit 1, "FAIL: a worker exited non-zero for a reason that is not the network"
# keep the work dir (the script rm -rf's it on EXIT) and read the failing w*.out:
#   podbox: GET https://public.ecr.aws/v2/docker/library/alpine/manifests/3.19:
#           HTTP 429: TOOMANYREQUESTS: Rate exceeded
```

### Suggested fix

Add `429|TOOMANYREQUESTS|rate` to the network-failure pattern in check 1, and have check 2 classify a holder that died with exit 125 before prune ran (its banner is in the log) as SKIP on hosts that cannot launch payloads, rather than FAIL. Both changes make the harness honest about what it measured, which is the script's own stated standard.

Environment: Linux 6.18.39, podbox 0.1.0 built from 1430040, 3 runs, one 429 each in checks 1; check 2 FAILed all 3 runs for the chroot reason above.

title: README quick start omits build-interpose.sh, so the first-run binary declines every dynamic payload; and no doc maps probe output to expected run behavior
body:
### The problem

The README's quick start cannot produce a binary that can run payloads on a glibc host, and nothing on the page says so:

```sh
./scripts/common/bootstrap-env.sh rust bloat cc zig tools
cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
./target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/podbox probe
./target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/podbox pull alpine:latest
./target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/podbox run alpine:latest /bin/echo hello
```

The interposer section below it says the interposer "builds once per libc" via `./scripts/build-interpose.sh`, but does not say that WITHOUT that step, `cargo build` embeds two empty placeholder objects and every `run` of a dynamically linked payload will decline with "interpose: declined" (honestly named, but still a decline a first-time user cannot distinguish from breakage). On the rung most hosts select, the interposer is not optional; the quick start treats it as an aside.

Second gap in the same page: the rung ladder ("would permit interpose" vs "enters chroot") and `PODBOX_MODE` are the two things a new user is most likely to misread (my own first run printed a 20-line banner and then failed to start the payload; the reason was my host, not podbox, but the README gave me no way to know that). One paragraph naming the three common cases (namespace host, chroot-capable host, chroot-denied host) and what `run` does on each would prevent it.

### What you have in mind

- Quick start step order: `build-interpose.sh` before `cargo build`, with one line on what a binary without embedded objects can and cannot do (`podbox system info` already prints "interposer: ..." and is the natural place to point).
- A three-line "which rung will I get" table under Status, keyed on the probe's own output, so the reader can map their probe result to expected `run` behavior before their first payload.

### What you tried instead

Followed the quick start verbatim on a fresh machine, hit "interpose: declined for ... statically linked" for a static payload (correct) and chroot EPERM for the default payload (my host's refusal, correctly reported by the banner, but unexplained by the README).

title: [T-1112] Deferred: Windows guest refused by name instead of implemented
body:
## Summary
T-1112 is partial, not done. It closes on the refusal arm of a dual-arm Prove. No guest path exists. This issue tells the implementer to study winquick first, try it, then implement the same shape on podbox's machine tier.

## Study winquick first (required before code)
Source: https://github.com/carlbomsdata/winquick, v0.5.1, Apache-2.0. Read in this order, then try the build below.

1. docs/architecture.md: two disks and no network. QEMU runs as a child process, never linked (GPLv2 boundary). Root disk is a disposable qcow2 overlay. Mailbox disk carries the command in and the results out. No SSH, no WinRM, no ports, no shared folders.
2. src/platform.rs: host decides guest. macOS arm64 goes qemu-system-aarch64 -M virt -accel hvf -cpu host to Windows ARM64. Windows x64 goes qemu-system-x86_64 -M q35 -accel whpx -cpu Nehalem to Windows x64. Linux goes -accel kvm with host CPU. Test the_accelerator_is_never_tcg asserts hvf, kvm, or whpx only. Software emulation is not the product.
3. src/qemu.rs boot_command: NVMe root plus NVMe mailbox (raw, writethrough) plus workspace plus artifacts plus capability disks, ramfb with display none, rtc localtime, no-reboot, serial log, QMP socket, optional -incoming for prepared state. NVMe because Validation OS has stornvme inbox; virtio-blk would need a driver before the guest can read its boot disk.
4. src/mailbox.rs plus guest/agent.cmd: 64 MiB MBR FAT32 image. Host writes WQMARK.TXT plus WQCMD.CMD plus WQGO.TXT with a nonce. Guest cmd.exe agent (AutoRun hook, WQ_ACTIVE guard) probes drives for the marker, remounts by volume GUID, runs the command in a child cmd.exe with stdin from NUL and stdout plus stderr redirected, writes WQOUT.TXT plus WQERR.TXT plus WQCODE.TXT with nonce, dismounts to flush, waits for the next command. WQCODE appearing is completion. No streaming by design; output arrives at shutdown.
5. Image pipeline in docs/architecture.md: user supplies Microsoft Validation OS ISO (about 2.4 GB, Microsoft licence, never redistributed). Setup converts VHDX to raw, adds wqagent.cmd plus AutoRun hive key with ntfscp plus hivexsh without mounting, writes base.qcow2 read-only. Prepared guest freezes booted RAM plus disk plus vars plus mailbox plus ready.json fingerprint. Warm path clones four files (APFS clone, about 4 ms), writes command, restores with -incoming, runs, kills, deletes. Cold path boots in about 11 s once. Failure layers fall back from resume to rebuild to cold boot.
6. Host support in README plus docs: macOS Apple Silicon HVF is the only supported host (100 runs cmd ver p50 310 ms). Windows WHPX boots but cold-boots every run (resumed guest waits 212 s for a 20 s timer, needs patched QEMU for migration blocker). Linux KVM builds and doctor reports correctly, but no Windows guest has been booted on physical Linux hardware, so guest execution is unverified.

## Try it (measured here, 2026-09-25)
Built from a clean clone on Linux x86_64 in 16.8 s with cargo build --release. Ran the built binary:

winquick doctor reports: cpu x86_64 kvm ok, os linux, qemu-system-x86_64 present at /usr/bin/qemu-system-x86_64 version 10.2.3 but too old (needs 11.0 or newer for NVMe migration, else every run boots cold), ntfscp plus ntfscat plus hivexsh missing (setup only), no Windows runtime (needs winquick setup with Microsoft ISO plus accept terms), UEFI firmware present at /usr/share/qemu/edk2-x86_64-code.fd, session none running, free space ok. /dev/kvm and /dev/net/tun are absent on this host. Exit 0 with 5 problems listed.

So the Linux path exists in the tree but is not runnable here: no accelerator, old QEMU, no helper tools, no licensed image. This is the exact constrained host podbox targets, and it is why a TCG shortcut is tempting and wrong: winquick rejects TCG as a different product (too slow to be interesting), and its Linux guest path is already the unverified one.

## What podbox actually does
Commit e4852f8 closes T-1112 with lifecycle::ensure_linux_guest at crates/podbox-cli/src/lifecycle.rs:1558, called from run.rs prepare for the requested platform and the stored record, from exec.rs for both checks, and from the start path. Linux passes, anything else exits 125 naming os and arch and the missing leg. Verified on beta 0.1.0-beta.7 (podbox-x86_64, sha ed6a6401):

podbox run --platform windows/amd64 any/image:tag cmd /c ver
podbox run: windows/amd64 is not a Linux guest. podbox runs Linux guests only: the chroot tier shares the host kernel and the machine tier boots Linux images. No windows guest support exists (TODO/milestones.md T-1112), so there is nothing to pull or enter for this platform
exit 125, no registry contacted, no store mutation.

Unit test a_non_linux_guest_is_refused_by_name watches fail then green. No QEMU Windows driver exists. The Prove has allowed either arm since 3c1211a, so the close is green per spec and partial per this issue.

1. Reopen T-1112 as partial. Keep the title. Add the decision underneath, never edit the Premise line (RULES section 5).
2. First target is Linux KVM Windows guest following winquick, not TCG: qemu-system-x86_64 -M q35 -accel kvm -cpu host, NVMe root overlay plus FAT mailbox plus workspace disk, cmd.exe agent via AutoRun, qcow2 backing chain with prepared state via migration, -nic none, base image read-only with per-run overlay discarded by Drop guard, streams plus exit code passed through with CRLF to LF as the only transform.

title: FR: streaming and chunked acquisition for lanes with a file-size ceiling (T-1112 follow-up)
body:
## FR: streaming and chunked acquisition for lanes with a file-size ceiling

Follow-up of T-1112 (PR 63). Recorded as an entry proposal, not
implemented in this pass.

### Problem

A lane with a hard `RLIMIT_FSIZE` cannot land any file at or over
the cap. Measured on the T-1112 lane: hard cap 1000000000 bytes,
unraiseable (EPERM even as uid 0), so the 2460880896-byte
ValidationOS ISO dies with SIGXFSZ at ~954 MB. The same wall
stands in front of every other large acquisition on such lanes:
OCI layer blobs pulled whole, base-image downloads, and any
provisioned disk whose data crosses the cap. A whole-file
download followed by a verify is the shape that breaks; the
failure (SIGXFSZ mid-transfer) is loud but late, after the
bandwidth is already spent.

### Proven pattern (PR 63, experiments 365)

Range-walk the origin, fetch only the bytes that matter, verify
as they arrive, never write a file the ceiling forbids:

- `fetch.rs` policy already owns two of the three bounds
  (declared length before the transfer, arriving bytes during
  it) plus digest and per-pid partial cleanup, tested with no
  network.
- 365 adds the third trick: parse the container on-origin
  (UDF walk by range request) and fetch one contiguous extent
  (abs LBA 1010, 910163968 bytes) instead of the 2.46 GB ISO.
- What is still missing is a native switch for it: today the
  range walk is a script around the fetch, not a mode of it.

### Proposal

1. `--stream` (name bikesheddable) on `podbox windows fetch`
   and on the image pull path: stream the body through the
   hasher to the destination with the running ceiling enforced,
   resume an interrupted transfer with `Range` instead of
   restarting it, and refuse up front where the declared length
   or the remaining room cannot hold the object.
2. Unify both pull paths on the `fetch.rs` policy: declared
   check, running check against `min(--max-bytes, RLIMIT_FSIZE,
   free space)`, digest pin, per-pid partials, nothing left
   behind on refusal. `podbox-image` blob writes need the same
   three bounds `fetch.rs` already has.
3. Pre-flight as a verdict, not a crash: read the ceiling and
   the free space before the first byte (365 does this after
   review caught its absence) and exit 2 where the lane cannot
   hold the object, so a small lane says so instead of dying
   at 95 percent.
4. Selective fetch where the container allows it: UDF extents
   (measured), and later OCI cross-repo mounts / partial blobs
   where the registry speaks ranges.

### Acceptance

- 365 re-driven green on a lane with a sub-object ceiling.
- A pull of a blob larger than the lane's ceiling either
  streams it under the ceiling or refuses up front naming the
  three numbers (object, ceiling, room); no partial survives
  either way.
- No new dependency: `ureq` range headers plus the existing
  policy code.

### Risks if wrong

Resume by `Range` assumes the origin honors ranges; a liar
that ignores `Range` and restarts the body must be detected
(comitted byte count jumps backwards) rather than appended
to. Digest stays mandatory on resumed transfers for the same
reason.

title: podssh: `podbox remote ssh`, a relay failover chain, and a server probe
body:
Builds on the podssh that was in flight and carries it further. The
transport, the rendezvous and the interop came from that work; this adds the
failure handling, the verb decision, the two measurements that changed the
shape of the thing, and a working session through the operator's own relay.

**Handoff for the next session: `docs/decisions/podssh-handoff.md`.** Read
that first. The useful half of it is the list of what is NOT proved and what
is blocked on whom; it is summarised at the bottom of this description too.

---

## Proved against `tcp.ssh.relay.ajam.dev`, 2026-09-27

Self-service tokens: `POST /v1/mint` with an empty body returns
`{token, expires, scope}`, the token is `ephm1.<exp>.forward.<mac>` and dies
at `expires`, never later than 72h after minting. The one used here was
minted in this session and expires 2026-09-30. **No token is in this tree**,
in any file, and `.gitignore` names the patterns that keep it that way.

The upgrade answers 101 with `X-Relay-Road: vpc`, `X-Relay-Target:
railway.new:22` and a `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` that matches, and the first
binary frame is `SSH-2.0-Go`. Through it: a full pubkey ssh session to a live
ephemeral VM, **exit 0**, `id -un` = root on Ubuntu 26.04.1; and an `scp`
upload, **exit 0**, content read back byte for byte.

### Using it found a real gap

`forward` reached one host:port through the egress proxy and took **no
relay**, so a `wss://` transport could not be handed to it at all. That is
exactly the shape the operator's relay is: it dials the target **itself** and
is addressed as `wss://host/connect/<host>/<port>`, so there is nobody to
pair with and `--name` has no meaning. A relay is one of two shapes and
conflating them left the second unreachable:

- a **rendezvous**: two named peers dial it and it pairs them. `connect` and
  `serve`, and sandssh's relay and `podssh relay`.
- a **forward**: the relay dials the target and the client only reaches the
  relay. `forward` with a relay.

They differ in exactly which hop is last, and they are one verb with different
arguments. `Chain` owns the failover so `connect` and `forward` make the same
decision about the same list, and each refusal is reported by name rather
than collapsing to "every relay failed".

The token travels in a **header**, not a query, which is the relay's own
preference as well as being right: a query string is written to every access
log on the way. The spec parser takes `?header=Name:Value` and validates the
name as an RFC 7230 token and the value against a newline, because a token is
operator-supplied text that lands in a request line and a newline there
smuggles a second header in.

## `podbox remote ssh`, not `podbox ssh`

`remote` is a **namespace**, not a synonym. `remote fetch`, `remote download`
and `remote wget` are all "reach a machine that is not this one" and each
would otherwise want its own top-level verb. `local` is the counterpart so
the axis is visible, and `machine ssh` is podman parity and a **different
axis**, so it stays separate. `podbox ssh` is refused with the group named
and exit 125, because an agent that typed it is asking a real question and
"unknown command" costs it a guess. The reasoning is in
`docs/decisions/remote-verb.md` and the e2e asserts both halves of the rename.

## A relay failover chain, because a shared public relay refuses in bursts

Measured 2026-09-27: in one window all three built-in public relays answered
502, 400 and 503 at once, and a later attempt in the same minute succeeded. A
client that names one relay is down for the length of that window however
healthy the code is. The chain tries N relays and reports every refusal by
name, so a bad relay costs one hop rather than the session.

Each hop gets its own full slice rather than a share of one global clock,
because a shared clock lets the first hop's latency starve every hop after
it. A wrong token is **not** retried down the list, because it cannot change.

The egress list is **ordered by measured first-byte latency**: 0.67s, 0.76s
and 4.34s to the same banner. The slowest was first in the first version of
the list, which is a latency bug rather than a style question: a client that
walks the list pays the first entry's latency before it reaches a good one,
and a ConnectTimeout was consumed before a fast relay was tried.

## The ssh server is probed, not assumed

`sshd -i -t` exiting 0 is not evidence that `sshd -i` runs, and the difference
produced the most misleading error this tool can emit. Measured 2026-09-27 in
the reference cage, in order:

1. `sshd -i -t -f <config>` exits **0**
2. `sshd -i` at runtime: `Privilege separation user nobody does not exist`
3. with a `nobody` entry: `Missing privilege separation directory: /var/chroot/ssh`
4. with `ChrootDirectory` moved: no effect, a different hardcoded path
5. with `UsePrivilegeSeparation no`: deprecated and **ignored** since OpenSSH 8.4

So no configuration makes a modern `sshd` run where chroot is denied, and a
default that picks it there fails with an error from the **far end**, which
reads as a podssh bug and is not one. `detect` now starts each candidate on a
throwaway socketpair and reports what it said.

The probe is the smallest thing that is true and says so: a server that exits
inside the window is a failure and its first line is the diagnosis, a server
still running is a pass, and it does **not** establish that the server speaks
ssh. Two stronger versions were written and both were wrong in a way a reader
would not have predicted. CPU time from `/proc` called `yes` healthy, because
with its stdout on a full socketpair it blocks in `write()` and burns nothing.
A "did it consume a byte" check refused `cat`, which is a working byte pipe
and is exactly what `--server cat` is for. A third hung the test binary on
`exec yes` and had to be killed with SIGTERM, so every operation on the probe
socket is non-blocking now.

## What a cage CAN run, proved rather than asserted

**dropbear, built dynamically** so the passwd shim reaches it, and tolerating
a denied `setgroups(2)`. A static dropbear carries its own libc, so it cannot
see that `root` exists and logs `Login attempt for nonexistent user` for a
user that is there. A full pubkey session over a rendezvous, in a cage with
**no pty, no bind, no chroot, no /var, no /etc/passwd, no UDP and no working
resolver**: ssh exit 0. That meets "no chroot tricks, and if we do, seamless"
by not chrooting at all.

The measurement, and what was **not** proved, are in
`docs/decisions/ssh-server-in-a-cage.md`.

## The e2e suite picks a server that runs

It hardcoded `sshd -i` in four places, and every one of those cases failed on
the reference cage while the transport was fine. Seven red results on a
machine where nothing was broken is "could not run must never read as denied"
wearing a different hat. `SSHD_CMD` is now chosen by what can start, and the
choice is printed with its reason.

## Experiments renumbered to 380-383

Main moved to `v0.1.0-beta.8` while this branch was open and took 369-372 for
the Windows lane drives. The gate's rule is that an experiment number is
never reused, because a citation of it has to keep meaning what it meant, so
the four podssh drives are now 380-383 and every citation follows,
self-references included. The INDEX and PROGRESS counts are re-derived by
`scripts/todo-count.py` rather than by hand.

## Proof

- `crates/podbox-ssh/tests/e2e.sh`: **13 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped**, in
  the reference cage. Four transports each against a byte pipe **and** against
  a real ssh client through a real `dropbear -i`; both verb checks; the three
  sandssh interop directions with the sandssh tree unchanged.
- The ajam relay: a full pubkey ssh session to a live ephemeral VM, exit 0,
  and an scp upload, exit 0, content verified.
- `cargo test -p podbox-ssh`: 53 unit tests.
- `scripts/check-todo.py`: green, 175 rows, 3 open, 1 partial.
- fmt and clippy clean on the touched crates.

## A builder and a CI for the ssh server a cage can run

`scripts/build-dropbear.sh` builds the server this tool actually uses, and
`.github/workflows/dropbear.yml` builds it on every run, asserts the three
properties that fail silently, and then **proves a real session** through the
artefact. A binary that compiles and cannot log anyone in is the failure this
exists to prevent, and `sshd -t` is exactly the check that cannot see it.

Two measured facts shape the build rather than a preference:

- **Dynamically linked, required not chosen.** A static dropbear carries its
  own libc, so `LD_PRELOAD` cannot reach it, its passwd lookups fail against a
  cage with no `/etc/passwd`, and it logs `Login attempt for nonexistent user`
  for a user that is there.
- **setgroups tolerant, setgid still fatal.** A seccomp-filtered cage denies
  `setgroups(2)`, so `initgroups()` always fails and dropbear exits on every
  login. `setgid` stays fatal because it is the call that changes the group
  and its failure is a real privilege problem; a denied `initgroups` leaves a
  session with correct uid and gid and no supplementary groups.

The pin is a **commit**, because upstream has no version tag: the first
version cloned `--branch 2026.94` and got `Remote branch 2026.94 not found`,
the version living in the source rather than in a ref. `BUILDINFO` records the
commit the build actually got, so a reader never has to trust the constant.

**Four defects, all found by running it, and three are the same mistake in
different clothes.** `strings | grep -q` under `set -o pipefail` reports
"absent" for a string that IS there: `grep -q` exits on the first match,
`strings` takes a SIGPIPE, and the pipeline returns 141. Measured: MATCH
without pipefail, NOMATCH with it, `rc=141` between. The assertion that used it
failed a correct build three times before the cause was found. The other two:
an assertion that read the setgid exit string backwards, and an `awk` with a
sticky flag that scanned to end-of-file and found a `dropbear_exit` belonging
to a different failure. A fourth, `set -u` making every unset optional
variable an error, was found only by a clean run, which is the argument for
running one.

A clean from-scratch build is in this branch's history: clone the pinned
commit, apply the patch, build, every assertion green, and then a full pubkey
session through the resulting binary, exit 0, uid 0.

## Docs that were run, and what running them found

`docs/decisions/podssh-getting-started.md` is a walk from nothing to a
session. Every command in it was executed and **three defects in `podssh
config` are the evidence**, because a guide written from reading a tool
documents the tool as imagined:

- it took positional arguments, which the verb does not, and failed with
  `--name is required` on a name it had just been given;
- it emitted a **bare `podssh`** in the ProxyCommand, which works in the
  terminal that generated the stanza and fails for every `ssh`, `scp` and
  `rsync` that reads it, because `ssh` runs a ProxyCommand through a login
  shell whose PATH is not the operator's. The code's own comment claimed an
  absolute path was the point and was not doing it;
- the stanza had **no trailing newline**, so it ran into whatever the reader
  appended and `ssh` reported a key verification failure on a line that was
  half a comment.

And one design gap rather than a typo: `config` generated `connect` for a
**forward** relay, which has nobody to pair with, so the stanza failed with
`--target is required`, naming a flag the reader never typed and no hint that
the verb was wrong. The generator now reads the relay's shape from its URL.

Proved: a stanza this generator produced, for the operator's relay, carries a
real pubkey session to a live ephemeral VM. `ssh -F <stanza> vm 'id -un'`
returns `root` and exits 0.

The guide also carries the two shell traps that cost time here, because both
produce a wrong answer rather than an error: `tr -d '\n'` before the sed that
extracts a token from pretty-printed JSON (without it the substitution passes
the whole body through: 159 characters beginning `{` instead of a 92-character
token), and the fact that `probe` prints JSON and nothing else, with `--json`
being the default rather than a switch.

---

## Handoff, condensed

**Read `docs/decisions/podssh-handoff.md` first.** The rest of this is the
short form.

**Not proved, and a later session must not assume it:**

- **No pty anywhere.** The cage has no `/dev/ptmx` and neither host can create
  one, so a full-screen TUI cannot run. The transport carries a one-shot
  command today; **T-1402 and T-1403** are the userspace line discipline that
  is what makes an operator's session feel native, and they are the first
  thing to pick up.
- **TURN is not wired in.** The crate has no TURN client. A TCP allocation
  needs a credential no account here can mint, and `exec://` is the documented
  route once one exists. The catalog records the endpoints so a later session
  does not rediscover them.
- **The three deep review passes on this branch have not been run.** The work
  is committed and tested, not reviewed. That is the first item on the
  handoff page, and the three questions are in `TODO/RULES.md` section 10.

**Settled, and not to be relitigated:** the verb is `podbox remote ssh`
(`docs/decisions/remote-verb.md`); the ssh server a cage can run is dropbear
built dynamically (`docs/decisions/ssh-server-in-a-cage.md`); relay ordering
is by measured latency, not discovery order; a relay token travels in a
header, not a query; and no token is committed anywhere, arriving in
`PODSSH_RELAY_TOKEN` instead, with the operator's relay tried **last** so a
session an uncredentialed relay can serve never waits for a credential that
may be absent.

**Blocked on a person:** nothing any more. The relay's tokens are self-service,
so the one thing that was blocked, a forward token, is now minted on demand.
